To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the aging process in nonhuman primates is associated with a progressive loss of dopamine neurons, which is accompanied by an increase in the vulnerability of the dopamine neurons to degeneration.
aging is the primary risk factor and the major determinant of vulnerability for developing PD.

aging is associated with increased markers of oxidative/nitrative stress and inflammation in the ventral midbrain of nonhuman primates and that these changes are most pronounced in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) dopamine neurons most vulnerable in PD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of aging as a risk factor for PD.
the role of aging in the development and progression of PD.
the role of aging in the etiology of PD and the mechanisms by which aging may predispose to PD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
aging is the most significant and consistent risk factor for PD.
aging represents a state of pre-PD, with the caveat that this pre-PD state is not a necessary precursor to PD.

aging and PD share a common biological pathway and that aging represents a pre-parkinsonism state, which is characterized by the presence of multiple biological markers that are associated with PD pathology and that increase with age.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the aging brain is a vulnerable brain.
the aging brain, in the case of dopamine neurons, is a pre-PD brain.
aging and PD are different sides of the same coin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the biology of the midbrain dopamine neurons in aging nonhuman primata is a pre-parkinson state, with the same biological changes that are seen in the dopamine neurons of patients with PD.
the biology of aging and PD are closely related, and that aging may represent biology accurately characterized by a pre-PD state, actively producing a state of vulnerability.
aging and PD are not two separate entities but two sides of the same coin.
